newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli shares end higher amid growing optimism.
newsitem.headline: Israeli shares end higher amid growing optimism.

text.p: Israeli shares rose strongly on Sunday and traders predicted the bullish mood would continue in the near term.

The benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 shares rose 1.22 percent, or 3.67 points, to 304.92 on all-share turnover of 202 million shekels against 318 million shekels on Thursday, the last day of trading before the Israeli weekend.
The Maof 25 blue-chip index closed 1.52 percent higher at 312.77.

"Investors are very optimistic and the mood is bullish," said Baruch Glicksberg at Clal Insurance. "The technical indicators are also supporting the positive trend. The market declined last week on low turnover and now it's rising with higher activity."

Yehuda Ben-Assayag, director-general at Koor Investment House, said the rising interest of foreign investors added to the positive mood. "The Koor deal shows that the Israeli market is underpriced and foreign investors are willing to pay more for Israeli shares."
Claridge Israel, controlled by Canada's Charles Bronfman, acquired 10 percent of Koor Industries from California investment company Shamrock Holdings in a deal announced on Tuesday.
Claridge paid about $185 million for the stake, representing about a 10 percent premium over Koor's market price.
Koor, the most active share, surged 5.0 percent to 39,373 agorot (Israeli cents) on volume of 12.8 million shekels.
Glicksberg said the main reason for the market's gain was the continued rise in the bond market.

"We expect redemptions of close to four billion shekels in long bonds but the government will issue bonds for only two billion shekels or even less. Part of the remaining money will find its way to the stock market," Glicksberg said.
Ben-Assayag said new money kept coming into the market. "The mutual funds (specialising in stocks) continue to attract new money and investors are showing more interest in the bourse," he said.

Glicksberg added that options prices reflected hope for continued gains. "The contracts are trading at a higher price than the market, reflecting expectations for a least another 0.5 percent rise on Monday," he said.
Traders said the market was also affected by the government's decision last week to cut the 1997 budget by 800 million shekels.

They added that the Bank of Israel was expected to leave its key lending rate for August unchanged at an annual 12.7 percent. The central bank will announce on Monday its monetary programme for August.

Makhteshim Chemical Works gained 0.25 percent to 2,424 agorot. Salomon Brothers downgraded Makhteshim from a strong buy to a buy due to a 178 percent appreciation in its stock price since August 1996.

The First International Bank of Israel, the main gainer on the Maof, surged 7.0 percent to 280,163. The bank said on Sunday it had signed an agreement with a consortium of international banks for a $120 million five-year loan.

Other active shares include Bezeq Israel Telecom, which gained 1.0 percent to 1,013 agorot on volume of 9.5 million shekels, and Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, which fell 0.75 percent to 22,353 agorot on turnover of 9 million shekels.
- Dan Gerstenfeld, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 x233
